simple: a piece of kernel work that can be paused and resumed, with its own place to keep its unfinished business.
analogy: a student with a notebook.
precise: an independently scheduled flow of execution in kernel mode, made of a control block (here struct Thread) and a private kernel stack; while it is not running, its register state is saved on that stack.
source: D3, R2 of F3-26 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the scratch memory a thread uses for function calls inside the kernel.
analogy: the student's own notebook.
precise: a region of kernel memory used as the call stack while the thread runs in ring 0; in this kernel 16 KiB (four 4 KiB pages) per thread, mapped in a slot of the stack area that starts at 4 GiB.
source: R2 of F3-26 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the line of threads that are ready to run and waiting for a CPU.
analogy: the queue of students waiting for the teacher.
precise: a data structure holding the threads in state Ready; here one global FIFO list protected by one spinlock.
source: D3 of F3-26 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: the thread a CPU runs when nobody else is ready; it sleeps until something happens.
analogy: the teacher marking papers until a hand goes up.
precise: a per-CPU thread that never blocks, which loops on "look for work, then sti; hlt"; it is never put in the run queue.
source: D1 of F3-26 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a finished thread whose memory has not been cleaned up yet.
analogy: a student who has gone home but whose notebook is still on the desk.
precise: a thread in state Dead that is still on the zombies list; its stack can be freed only by another thread, because a thread cannot free the stack it is running on.
source: R2 of F3-26 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a spinlock that serves waiters in arrival order.
analogy: numbered tickets at the office desk.
precise: a spinlock with two counters: next (atomically incremented to take a ticket) and serving (incremented on release); a CPU enters when serving equals its ticket, so the lock is first-come, first-served.
source: D3, R2 of F3-27 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a lock taken with interrupts switched off on this CPU, because an interrupt handler also takes it.
analogy: the bell may not ring while you hold the sheet.
precise: lock_irqsave() saves RFLAGS and executes cli before taking the lock; unlock_irqrestore() releases it and restores the saved interrupt flag. Any lock that an interrupt handler takes must be taken this way everywhere else.
source: D3, R3 of F3-27 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: a counter of spinlocks held by this CPU; while it is above zero the scheduler must not switch threads.
analogy: "do not move the student while they hold the sheet".
precise: Cpu::preempt_count, incremented by Spinlock::lock and decremented by unlock; trap_dispatch preempts only when it is zero (F3-26).
source: R2 of F3-27 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: waiting a moment before going to sleep, if the holder is busy on another CPU.
analogy: if the person with the sheet is writing right now, waiting a few seconds is cheaper than sitting down.
precise: before sleeping, Mutex::lock spins up to 2000 iterations while the owner thread is in state Running; sleeping and waking cost a switch each.
source: R2 of F3-27 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: debug code that remembers which locks were taken while others were held and complains about the reverse order.
analogy: a hall monitor who writes down who held which book first.
precise: here lockdep_check_order: per thread, the lock classes held; globally, a table before[a][b]; the first acquisition of a while holding b after before[a][b] was set is reported. Linux's "lockdep" is a far larger version of the same idea.

simple: a timer inside the spin loop that gives up after too long and prints who holds what.
analogy: the caretaker at night.
precise: Spinlock::lock measures its wait with the TSC and calls lockup() after 2000 ms; the first CPU to report prints every CPU's thread, interrupt depth, awaited lock and held locks, then panics.

simple: several CPUs sharing one memory and running one kernel.
analogy: several teachers in one school, one timetable.
precise: a system in which all processors have equal access to memory and devices and any of them can run any kernel or user code.

simple: the one CPU that starts running at power-on.

simple: every other CPU, asleep until the kernel wakes it.
analogy: the new teachers at home.

simple: the three messages that wake an AP and tell it where to start.
analogy: "wake up", then "come in at side door 8", said twice.
precise: an INIT inter-processor interrupt, a delay, then two start-up IPIs whose vector field gives the 4 KiB page at which the AP starts executing in real mode (vector 0x08 = address 0x8000 in this kernel).

simple: a small piece of start-up code copied below 1 MiB, where a CPU in 16-bit mode can reach it.
analogy: the side door and the staircase to the staff room.
precise: code that takes an AP from real mode through protected mode to long mode with the BSP's page tables, then jumps to the kernel's C++ entry (trampoline.S).

simple: variables that exist once per CPU, so each CPU has its own copy.
analogy: each teacher's desk drawer.
precise: here the Cpu structure (current thread, idle thread, tick count, preemption count, GDT, TSS, double-fault stack); each CPU's GS base register points at its own, and %gs:0 holds its address.

simple: a register that adds an offset to every memory access that uses the GS segment.
analogy: "your drawer" means a different drawer for each teacher.
precise: in 64-bit mode, the base of the GS segment, set through a model-specific register; mov %gs:0, %rax reads the first 8 bytes of this CPU's Cpu.

simple: an interrupt one CPU sends to another.
analogy: the principal phoning a teacher.
precise: a message sent by writing the local APIC's interrupt command register (ICR): destination APIC id, vector or special type (INIT, SIPI). This kernel uses vector 0xF0 for TLB shootdown and 0xF1 for "reschedule".

simple: telling every CPU to forget a translation that was just removed.
analogy: phoning every teacher to tear up one sticky note.
precise: after changing or removing a page-table entry, invalidating it locally (invlpg) and sending an IPI to every other CPU that may cache it, whose handler invalidates it too; the initiator waits until all have acknowledged before the old frame may be reused.

simple: an old translation a CPU still uses after the page table changed.
analogy: an out-of-date sticky note.
precise: a TLB entry that no longer matches the page tables; the CPU keeps using it until it is invalidated or evicted, so reads and writes reach the old frame.

simple: one CPU holds A and waits for B while another holds B and waits for A.
analogy: two students each holding a book the other needs.
precise: a deadlock whose wait-for graph is a two-lock cycle; possible whenever two code paths take the same two locks in opposite orders and can run in parallel.

simple: how much the code currently running is allowed to do.
analogy: staff or student.
precise: on x86, the current privilege level (CPL) is the low two bits of CS: 0 for the kernel, 3 for user code; privileged instructions and supervisor pages fault at CPL 3.

simple: the fast "enter kernel" and "return to user" instructions of x86-64.
analogy: the window's hatch, opening and closing.
precise: SYSCALL saves RIP in RCX and RFLAGS in R11, masks RFLAGS with FMASK, loads kernel CS/SS from STAR and jumps to LSTAR; SYSRET reverses it, loading user CS/SS from another field of STAR. Neither switches the stack.

simple: a numbered CPU configuration register, read and written with special instructions.
analogy: the settings panel in the caretaker's room.
precise: registers accessed with rdmsr/wrmsr by number in ECX; here EFER, STAR, LSTAR, FMASK, GS base and kernel GS base.
source: D3 of F3-29 (pending verification; book and specification sources title only, dossier gate G1 open; R = lab runs in this build)

simple: an instruction that swaps the user's GS base with the kernel's.
analogy: swapping the student's badge for the staff badge at the door.
precise: exchanges the GS base with the IA32_KERNEL_GS_BASE MSR, so that on entry from ring 3 %gs points at this CPU's Cpu (F3-28) and on exit back at the user's value.

simple: the CPU refuses to run user-page code while in kernel mode.
analogy: staff never follow instructions written in a student's notebook.
precise: Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention, CR4 bit 20: an instruction fetch at CPL 0 from a user page faults.

simple: the CPU refuses kernel reads and writes of user pages, except inside an explicitly opened window.
analogy: staff hands do not work in student bags unless the copy procedure is opened.
precise: Supervisor Mode Access Prevention, CR4 bit 21: data accesses at CPL 0 to user pages fault unless RFLAGS.AC is set, which stac sets and clac clears.

simple: checking that an address and a length given by a user program describe only that program's memory.

simple: a list of instructions that are allowed to fault, and where to continue if they do.

precise: pairs (faulting RIP, fixup RIP) in the section .uaccess_fixups; the page-fault handler, on a kernel-mode fault, looks the RIP up and resumes at the fixup, which returns an error.

simple: a 64-bit address whose top bits are all copies of bit 47.

simple: the kernel code that reads a program file and sets up memory so the program can run.
